chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Commodities Are and Why They Trade

lessons.title: Why Investors Hold Commodities: Inflation, Diversification and the Rupee

children.text: Think back to 2008. The Nifty 50 closed 2007 at about 6,139 and ended 2008 at about 2,959, a fall of roughly 52%. In the same year, the rupee price of gold rose sharply, because global gold held up while the rupee slid from about ₹39 to about ₹49 per dollar. A family that held some gold alongside its shares had one asset going up while the other collapsed. That, in one year, is the case for holding commodities. By the end of this lesson you will know the three real reasons investors hold commodities (inflation, diversification and the rupee), the maths behind each, and the situations where those reasons break down.

body.text: You do not hold commodities because they compound like businesses. They do not. You hold them because they tend to rise in the exact situations that hurt your other investments: commodity-driven inflation, a falling rupee and a crisis in equity markets.

children.text: Reason 1: Protection Against Inflation

markDefs.definition: The headline percentage return on an investment, before adjusting for inflation or tax.
Your return after subtracting inflation. It measures the change in what your money can actually buy.

children.text: Inflation is the silent tax on every rupee you hold. What matters is not your
nominal return
but your
real return
, what your money can buy after prices rise.

body.caption: A close approximation for low rates. The exact version is (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) minus 1.

children.text: Here is why that matters for a typical Indian saver. Take a fixed deposit paying 7% a year, held by someone in the 30% tax slab, in a year when CPI inflation runs at 6%.
Pre-tax real return: 7% minus 6% = about 1%
Post-tax nominal return: 7% × (1 minus 0.30) = 4.9%
Post-tax real return: 4.9% minus 6% = about minus 1.1%

body.text: Commodities are not just protection against inflation. Often they are the cause of it. When crude oil, edible oil or vegetables spike, CPI follows. Owning some of the things whose prices are rising is a direct offset to the rising cost of living. This works best for supply-shock inflation, and far less reliably when inflation comes from wages or easy credit.

children.text: 2022 shows the idea in action. Brent crude spiked to around $139 a barrel in March, Indian CPI inflation hit 7.79% in April, and the Nifty 50 returned only about 4% for the full calendar year, closing near 18,105 against about 17,354 a year earlier. An investor who held energy exposure had something rising while inflation ate into everything else.

body.title: Your real FD return
body.prompt: Meera, a Pune-based chartered accountant in the 30% tax slab, has an FD paying 7.5%. CPI inflation for the year is 5%. Ignoring cess, what is her approximate post-tax real return, in percent?
body.explanation: Post-tax return = 7.5% × 0.70 = 5.25%. Subtract 5% inflation to get about 0.25%. Her money barely keeps pace with prices, even though the headline rate looks healthy.

children.text: Reason 2: Diversification

markDefs.definition: A number from minus 1 to plus 1 showing how closely two assets move together. Plus 1 means in lockstep, 0 means unrelated, minus 1 means opposite.

children.text: Diversification only works if your assets do not all fall together. The measure of that is
correlation

. Two Nifty 50 index funds from different AMCs are almost perfectly correlated, so owning both adds nothing. Gold has historically had low correlation with Indian equities, and in several sharp equity sell-offs it has moved the other way.
Watch what a small allocation does in a bad year. Suppose equities fall 30% and gold rises 20%. These are illustrative numbers, not a forecast.

body.caption: Portfolio return is the weighted average of each asset's return, where w is the share of the portfolio.

body.title: Illustrative crash year: equities minus 30%, gold plus 20%

children.text: A 10% gold allocation cut the loss from 30% to 25%. That sounds modest, but it changes the recovery maths. After a 30% fall you need about 43% just to get back to where you started. After a 25% fall you need about 33%.

body.title: Blend the portfolio
body.prompt: Arjun holds 80% in a Nifty 50 index fund and 20% in a gold ETF. In a bad year, the index fund falls 20% and the gold ETF rises 15%. What is his total portfolio return, in percent?
body.explanation: (0.80 × minus 20%) + (0.20 × 15%) = minus 16% + 3% = minus 13%. The gold slice absorbed 7 percentage points of the equity damage.

body.text: Correlations are not constant. In a panic, investors sell whatever they can, and in March 2020 gold dipped alongside equities before rallying to record highs by August. Diversification reduces damage over a full cycle. It does not guarantee that something in your portfolio goes up every single month.

children.text: Reason 3: A Hedge Against the Rupee

Gold, silver, crude oil and base metals are priced globally in US dollars. An Indian investor earns two returns on them at once: the change in the dollar price, and the change in the rupee against the dollar. When the rupee weakens, rupee prices rise even if nothing happens globally.

body.caption: R_USD/INR is the percentage change in rupees per dollar. A positive number means the rupee weakened.

children.text: The long-run direction is clear. The rupee has weakened from under ₹50 per dollar in 2008 to above ₹85 by the end of 2024, with sharp episodes such as the 2013 "taper tantrum", when it fell to around ₹68 per dollar in August. Every one of those moves quietly lifted the rupee price of dollar-priced commodities.

body.title: Show me the math: two returns stacked together

children.text: Say gold rises 10% in dollar terms over a year, and USD/INR moves from 84 to 88.2, a 5% weakening of the rupee.
Growth from gold: 1.10
Growth from the currency: 88.2 ÷ 84 = 1.05
Combined: 1.10 × 1.05 = 1.155, a return of 15.5% in rupees

Simply adding 10% and 5% gives 15%. The extra 0.5% is the currency gain earned on top of the gold gain. Now reverse it: if gold rises 10% but the rupee strengthens 5%, the rupee return is 1.10 × 0.95 minus 1 = 4.5%.

body.title: Which year is best for an Indian gold holder?
body.question: In which of these situations does an Indian investor earn the highest rupee return on gold?
options: Gold up 8% in dollars, rupee strengthens 3%
Gold up 5% in dollars, rupee weakens 4%
Gold flat in dollars, rupee weakens 6%
Gold up 10% in dollars, rupee strengthens 2%
body.explanation: Option A: 1.08 × 0.97 = 4.8%. Option B: 1.05 × 1.04 = 9.2%. Option C: 1.00 × 1.06 = 6%. Option D: 1.10 × 0.98 = 7.8%. A modest gold rise plus a weaker rupee beats a bigger gold rise with a stronger rupee.

children.text: Which Commodity Hedges What

body.caption: What each commodity group tends to protect against, and where it fails

cells: The rupee weakens, fear rises, real interest rates fall
Real interest rates rise sharply, the dollar strengthens, risk appetite is strong
Gold rallies and industrial demand is strong at the same time
Industrial demand slows; it swings harder than gold both ways
Supply shocks, wars and sanctions push up energy-driven inflation
Global demand slumps, as in 2020, or producers flood supply
Global growth and construction are booming
Bumper harvests, export curbs or stock limits cap prices

children.text: Notice that no single commodity hedges everything. Gold is the one most Indian investors actually hold for the long term, because it addresses all three reasons at once and has no expiry, no storage headache when held through an ETF, and no dependence on a harvest.
The Case Against: When Commodities Let You Down

body.title: Good reasons vs bad reasons to hold commodities

columns.label: Good reasons
points: A modest allocation to offset equity and currency risk
A long-term hedge against rupee depreciation
A deliberate, sized trade with defined risk

columns.label: Bad reasons
points: A relative made money in silver last year
Buying crude because it is on the news
Replacing your equity SIP with commodity futures

children.text: No income.
Commodities pay no dividends or interest. Over decades, a productive business should beat a lump of metal.
Long flat stretches.
Gold peaked near $1,921 an ounce in September 2011 and fell to about $1,050 by December 2015. In rupee terms, it went roughly nowhere between 2012 and 2018.
Decades-long drawdowns are possible.
Gold's January 1980 peak of about $850 an ounce was not surpassed in dollar terms until 2008.
Holding costs for futures.
Long-term exposure through futures means rolling contracts every expiry, which can cost money in some market structures. You will learn why in Chapter 2.

body.title: An illustrative diversified portfolio (not a recommendation)

body.label: The allocation question
body.value: Commodities are a satellite, not the core
body.context: Many long-term investors treat gold as a single-digit to low-teens percentage of their portfolio. The right number depends on your goals and risk profile, which is a question for a SEBI-registered investment adviser.

body.title: The gold enthusiast
body.scenario: Vikram, a 52-year-old business owner in Surat with a ₹4 crore portfolio, watched gold hit record highs. He is thinking of moving 50% of his portfolio into gold and silver, saying: "Gold protects against inflation, the rupee always falls, and stocks are too risky."
body.prompt: What is right about Vikram's reasoning, and what is he missing?
body.modelAnswer:
What he gets right: gold does hedge rupee weakness and some kinds of inflation, and it has diversified Indian equity portfolios in several crises, including 2008.

What he is missing:
1. Timing risk. Moving half his wealth after a big rally means buying at record prices. Gold went roughly nowhere in rupee terms from 2012 to 2018 after its last big run.
2. No income. Half his portfolio would generate no dividends or interest, which matters as he approaches retirement.
3. The rupee does not "always" fall. It moves in both directions over shorter periods, and a strengthening rupee cuts gold returns in India.
4. Silver is not a safe asset. It swings much harder than gold because of its industrial demand.
5. Concentration. A hedge is meant to be a slice, not half the portfolio. Replacing diversification with a single big bet defeats the purpose.

body.title: Name the concept
body.textWithBlank: Your return after subtracting inflation, which tells you what your money can actually buy, is called your ___ return.
body.explanation: The real return is the number that matters. A 7% FD with 6% inflation is only about a 1% real return before tax.

cards.definition: Return after subtracting inflation; approximately nominal return minus inflation.
The headline return before adjusting for inflation or tax.
How closely two assets move together, from minus 1 (opposite) to plus 1 (in lockstep).
Inflation caused by a sudden shortage of key goods like crude oil or food, where commodities tend to hedge best.
Holding dollar-priced assets like gold, whose rupee value rises when the rupee weakens.
The weighted average of each holding's return, using its share of the portfolio as the weight.

points: Investors hold commodities for three reasons: inflation protection, diversification and a hedge against the rupee.
Real return, not headline return, is what counts. A 7% FD can lose purchasing power after tax in a 6% inflation year.
Commodities hedge supply-shock inflation best, because they are often the cause of it.
A small allocation to a low-correlation asset like gold can meaningfully reduce losses in an equity crash.
Indian investors earn the dollar price change plus the rupee move: (1 + dollar return) × (1 + currency change) minus 1.
Commodities pay no income and can go nowhere for years, so they belong in a portfolio as a satellite, not the core.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Historical figures are approximate and past performance does not indicate future returns. Portfolio allocations shown are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making allocation decisions.
